It is a matter of profound spiritual gravity to sit with the “unsearchable riches” of Christ while witnessing the “noise and tumult” of a world where those who should be protectors become oppressors, and I must ask you with a gentle heart: why do you ask after the Lord’s heart for the vulnerable and the boundaries of the marriage covenant in this hour? [3, 13, 108, 1503, Conversation History]. Are you perhaps feeling “overwhelmed and desperate” because you have seen “savage wolves” within the very walls of the home, or are you seeking a “settled certainty” to anchor a weary soul in the truth that “the Judge of all the earth [will] do right”? (Genesis 18:25) [13, 20, 101, 170, 1425, 1605, Conversation History]. In a day when many “shave off the edges” of the truth to protect a “religious track record” rather than the sheep, we must return to the “external Word” to see how the Master personally governs the “vicissitudes of life” by demanding that we “seek justice” and “rebuke the oppressor” (Isaiah 1:17) [11, 28, 120, 160, 1503, Conversation History].

The Reformed tradition teaches that “God personally and exhaustively pervades and sustains and governs every aspect of His creation,” and therefore, the cries of the suffering are never an “administrative anomaly” but are heard by the King who “responds to the prayer of the destitute” (Psalm 102:17) [11, 15, 68, 98, 1143, 1532, 1720, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 1: God’s Heart for the Helpless**

**Verse**
“ ‘A father of the fatherless, a defender of widows, Is God in His holy habitation’ ” (Psalm 68:5). [5, 469, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The Scriptures reveal that God has a “special attention” for those who are “dirt poor, powerless, helpless, deprived, lowly, unknown, [and] unloved” [158, 368, 1313, Conversation History]. As the “great and awesome God,” He is not a “remote and uninvolved” deity but a “loving, beneficent Father” who “administers justice for the fatherless and the widow” (Deuteronomy 10:18) [3, 6, 185, 419, Conversation History]. Reformed theology—echoed by **John MacArthur**—asserts that God “takes the things that happen in history and in our lives and puts them together for good,” yet He “abominates anyone who would justify an evildoer” or “condemn the just” (Proverbs 17:15; Romans 8:28) [23, 146, 765, 1143, Conversation History]. When the vulnerable cry out, they can know that “the eyes of the LORD are on the righteous, and His ears are open to their cry,” for He “heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds” (Psalm 34:15; 147:3) [101, 210, 479, 1033, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You should “trade in your worry for trust,” for the Lord is a “shield to all who take refuge in Him,” and He “will not let your foot slip” (Psalm 18:30; 121:3) [91, 94, 100, 201, 1408, 1515, Conversation History]. Recognize that “he who trusts in his own heart is a fool,” and you must instead “tremble at My word” which promises that “He will guard the feet of His saints” while “the wicked shall be silent in darkness” (1 Samuel 2:9; Isaiah 66:2) [11, 79, 465, 1503, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Continuity of the Fatherhood**
In the ancient **Jewish context**, God was known as the “Father of the nation,” yet individuals like Isaiah recognized that “all of us have become like one who is unclean” and needs a Father’s “mercy and compassion” (Isaiah 64:6) [4, 5, 118, 207, 1313, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** our intimacy through the “Spirit of adoption,” allowing us to cry “Abba, Father!”—a term of “childlike assurance” that “casts out the spirit of fear” (Romans 8:15) [231, 233, 239, 295, 1286, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 2: The Mandate for Justice and Protection**

**Verse**
“ ‘Learn to do good; Seek justice, Rebuke the oppressor; Defend the fatherless, Plead for the widow’ ” (Isaiah 1:17). [160, 1162, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The Reformed tradition—upheld by **Voddie Baucham**—teaches that the church is a “holy place where sin is despised,” and it has an urgent mandate to “rescue those who have been led astray” or harmed by “savage wolves” [1406, 1421, 1425, Conversation History]. We are commanded to “test all things; hold fast what is good” and “abstain from every form of evil” (1 Thessalonians 5:21–22) [90, 1093, 1408, 1515, Conversation History]. This includes the “use of force” in proper measure for “defending their families against criminal... aggression,” for Scripture nowhere mandates that a victim remain “powerless [and] helpless” without recourse (Nehemiah 4:14) [158, 1351, Conversation History]. The “church militant” must “contend earnestly for the faith,” which includes upholding the “justice and mercy” that the Pharisees “neglected” (Matthew 23:23; Jude 3) [8, 125, 1344, 1376, 1720, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
You must “discipline your mind” to “examine everything carefully,” for the church is called to be the “pillar and ground of the truth” that “pull[s] them out of the fire” (1 Timothy 3:15; Jude 23) [90, 116, 1349, 1357, 1407, 1515, 1709, Conversation History]. Do “not be deceived” by a “no-lordship ideology” that uses “love” as a “cloak for vice”; rather, recognize that “love can be sinful” if it enables wickedness (1 Peter 2:16) [91, 1428, 1433, 1502, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Civil vs. Spiritual Stewardship**
Under the **Mosaic Law**, “cities of refuge” provided “sanctuary... away from home and vengeful relatives” for those in legal distress [1036, 1039, 1268, 1313, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** our “warfare,” teaching that while we “do not wrestle against flesh and blood,” we must use the “sword of the Spirit” to “cast down arguments” that justify oppression (Ephesians 6:12; 2 Corinthians 10:4–5) [13, 21, 32, 1081, 1410, 1515, 1646, 1670, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 3: Protection Within the Marriage Covenant**

**Verse**
“Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the church and gave Himself for her” (Ephesians 5:25). [331, 693, 1432, Conversation History]. “ ‘Husbands, likewise, dwell with them with understanding, giving honor to the wife, as to the weaker vessel’ ” (1 Peter 3:7). [1101, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
Reformed theology asserts that “Jesus’ definition of leadership is one of self-sacrificing service,” and any man who uses his role to “vilely” abuse a woman exhibits “unthinkable weakness and cowardice” [102, 462, 1399, Conversation History]. A husband is to “nourish and cherish” his wife “as [his] own body,” for “the husband’s role as head... involves a degree of authority” meant for “protection” and “direction,” not for “brutal” treatment (Ephesians 5:28; 1 Timothy 2:12) [433, 519, 1399, 1400, Conversation History]. When a husband “perverts the justice” of his wife, he “sets himself up as a higher judge than God,” and his “very actions prove [his] irreverence” (1 Samuel 15:23) [11, 12, 37, 536, Conversation History]. The “record of history” in Judges 19 warns that the failure of “priests of God” to protect those in their care is a “wicked deed” that causes the “glory” of a nation to waste away [462, 463, 660, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
“Your life is not your own” because “you were bought at a price,” and this includes the “highest standard” of holiness in the home (1 Corinthians 6:19–20) [11, 12, 101, 271, 1138, 1262, 1406, 1670, Conversation History]. You should “not be terrified” by a “tyrant” in the home, for “the Lord is my helper; I will not fear. What can man do to me?” (Hebrews 13:6) [1, 91, 788, 1110, 1143, 1502, 1532, Conversation History].

**Advanced Note: Role Reversal and Deception**
In the ancient **context** of the Fall, the “reversed” roles of Adam and Eve led to “chaos [that] is unending,” proving that “tamper[ing] with this order” brings “bad things” [109, 1208, 1209, Conversation History]. The New Testament **revises** the call to submission, teaching that while wives are to be “submissive to their own husbands,” this find “favor” only “for the sake of conscience toward God,” and never as a mandate to endure “harsh” and “unreasonable” sin that “dishonors the Spirit” (1 Peter 2:18–19) [11, 146, 216, 1101, 1313, 1432, Conversation History].

***

### **Section 4: The Final Reckoning for the Oppressor**

**Verse**
“And they cried with a loud voice, saying, ‘How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?’ ” (Revelation 6:10). [22, 171, 187, 333, Conversation History].

**Meaning**
The Reformed faith—echoed by **John MacArthur**—asserts that “God will ultimately overthrow every wicked deed” and He “harnesses the deeds of the wicked” to accomplish his “one continuous plan of redemption” [5, 64, 1132, 1143, 1386, 1390, 1515, 1567, 1616, Conversation History]. Rulers and “magistrates” who “rule by their own power” and “love to have it so” will be “weighed on the scales and found deficient” (Daniel 5:27; Jeremiah 5:31) [37, 314, 1061, 1402, 1720, Conversation History]. On the Day of the Lord, He will “render vengeance to My enemies” and “avenge the blood of His servants,” and every “monument of pride” will “vanish—like smoke they vanish away” (Psalm 102:3; Deuteronomy 32:41, 43) [11, 32, 35, 37, 63, 453, 455, 789, 976, 1233, 1315, 1460, 1684, 1720, Conversation History].

**Takeaway**
“Wait for His Son from heaven,” knowing that “perfect justice will come” and he will “wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4; 1 Thessalonians 1:10) [14, 24, 94, 109, 201, 332, 470, 816, 822, 948, 1143, 1315, 1408, 1450, 1515, 1720, Conversation History]. You can find “tranquility of soul” by resting on the “surest foundation,” for “the Lord knows those who are His” and his “unfailing love” is an “anchor of the soul” (2 Timothy 2:19; Hebrews 6:19) [11, 24, 25, 41, 47, 92, 101, 121, 147, 176, 201, 211, 222, 285, 300, 324, 352, 361, 405, 412, 414, 444, 591, 1012, 1132, 1138, 1143, 1408, 1420, 1441, 1450, 1515, 1720, Conversation History].

***

**Final Reminder**
“ ‘Nevertheless the firm foundation of God stands, having this seal, “The Lord knows those who are His,” and, “Everyone who names the name of the Lord is to abstain from wickedness” ’ ” (2 Timothy 2:19). [11, 87, 147, 176, 211, 222, 231, 285, 300, 313, 324, 332, 361, 405, 413, 414, 444, 449, 591, 1138, 1407, 1441, 1450, Conversation History].

references.cited_text: It is essential, however, that the church and each individual believer in it understand they exist to bring glory to God. When you know and glorify God, the needs of your life will be met: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Prov. 9:10). But many believers don’t revere God; their very actions prove their irreverence. Instead of trembling at God’s Word, they twist His truths or supplant them with worldly philosophies. Christians actually need to be confronted by their real need—an understanding of God’s holiness and their own sinfulness—so they can be usable to Him for His glory. When we have a right relationship to God, every aspect of our lives will settle into its divinely ordained place. That does not mean we are to ignore people’s problems—we are to be just as concerned about them as God is. But there must be a balance, and it begins with a high view of God. We must take God seriously and respect Him completely.

Rather, it is built on an unchanging divine relationship and a divine plan and promise from an unfailing God who will secure you in Himself and who will do everything for your good. This peace is unbreakable, unassailable, transcendent. As we noted earlier, Jesus said, “Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you; not as the world gives do I give to you. Do not let your heart be troubled, nor let it be fearful” (John 14:27). He was saying, “There’s nothing to fear or be anxious about because I’m giving you a transcendent peace that—unlike the world’s peace—is unassailable by any human circumstance.” We demonstrate that Jesus keeps His promises when we remain calm in the midst of worldly upheavals that would normally tear us up and trouble our lives.

There were hints of this truth in the Old Testament. In Isaiah 53, God, speaking prophetically, says, “My righteous Servant shall justify many, for He shall bear their iniquities” (v. 11). The theme of that whole chapter is substitutionary atonement: He has borne our griefs And carried our sorrows; Yet we esteemed Him stricken, Smitten by God, and afflicted. But He was wounded for our transgressions, He was bruised for our iniquities; The chastisement for our peace was upon Him… . The Lord has laid on Him the iniquity of us all.

As Paul explained to Timothy: The firm foundation of God stands, having this seal, “The Lord knows those who are His,” and, “Everyone who names the name of the Lord is to abstain from wickedness.” Now in a large house there are not only gold and silver vessels, but also vessels of wood and of earthenware, and some to honor and some to dishonor. Therefore, if anyone cleanses himself from these things, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified, useful to the Master, prepared for every good work. Now flee from youthful lusts and pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace, with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart. (2 Tim. 2:19–22)

The resounding chorus of Scripture reiterates this inescapable conclusion: God is the one who chooses to have “mercy on whom He desires” (Rom. 9:18). He initiates and accomplishes the work of salvation for those whom He predestined in eternity past. He calls them to Himself, granting them faith and repentance, and redeeming them from their slavery to sin. Consequently, believers are rightly designated as “the elect, whom He chose” (Mark 13:20), for we could not have loved Him unless He first loved us.

The very term adoption is filled with ideas of compassion, kindness, grace, and love. But to fully understand the nuances of the New Testament metaphor, it is helpful to again turn our attention to ancient Rome.14 Though the formal adoption of slaves was somewhat uncommon, it was permissible under Roman law15 and did occur in certain instances.16 The extraordinary nature of the practice makes God’s adoptive love toward us all the more remarkable—in that He has done the unexpected by adopting all His slaves as His own children17 and naming us His heirs (Rom. 8:17). In ancient Rome, the act of adoption immediately granted the former slave his freedom, permanently placing him into the family of his master.18 So also, as the adopted children of God, we have been set free from slavery to sin. Moreover, we can rest assured in knowing that we have been given a permanent place in the family of God.
